editorial:
Imagine growing up in New York City during the 80s, where who you hang out with can cause a huge fight at home. You follow a young Jewish boy who finds a best friend in a rebellious Black classmate. While the two kids just want to be buddies, the boy's wealthy family is not happy about it. It feels like a cozy but tense look at childhood, showing how kids often see the world much more clearly than adults do. The vibe is very grounded and realistic, making you feel like you are walking through the streets of Queens right along with them.

The acting is the best part here, as the kids feel totally natural and not like they are reading from a script. The story moves a bit slowly, which might bore some people, but it helps you really feel the friendship growing. If you like stories about friendship and unfairness, you will love this.
endingExplained: As the movie wraps up, you see the boys grow apart because the world around them is too harsh. The ending shows that while their bond was real, the pressure from their families and the racism of the city eventually pulled them in different directions. It finishes on a sad but honest note, reminding you that some childhood friendships are beautiful even if they do not last forever into adulthood.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves heartfelt stories about friendship and growing up.
